reported_as: Supplemental Material Sec. I.B: To further reduce the computational cost, we impose full translational invariance on the f_ij parameters by considering a f_ij sublattice. When this sublattice contains M spins, the number of independent variational parameters f_ij is reduced to M × Ns ∼ O(Ns), whereas without assuming translational symmetry, the number of f_ij is (Ns × Ns) ∼ O(Ns^2). ... We therefore take M = 16 in simulations of the 3D pyrochlore lattice, while M = 2 × 2 × 16 = 64 for simulations of the quasi-2D super-tetrahedron square lattice (STSL). ... Sec. I.E: These parameters are optimized by the natural gradient (or equivalently stochastic reconfiguration) method [12-14] with the help of the conjugate gradient method [12, 15]. This allows us to access system sizes as large as Ns = 1024 sites by reducing memory and computational cost [2]. ... Sec. I.G: In principle, higher-power Lanczos steps are possible and will improve the energy even further, however are very costly, which is the reason why we consider only the first-step Lanczos method in this work. ... SM Sec. V: Linear extrapolation to zero variance has been done for 20 to 40 statistically independent measurements of the energy-eigenvalues from a singly optimized wave function within mVMC and mVMC-RBM, in combination with the first Lanczos step. ... method: SSE QMC (stochastic series expansion), T -> 0 converged at beta/L = 32 and 64
reference: Sandvik, High-precision ground state parameters of the two-dimensional spin-1/2 Heisenberg model on the square lattice, arXiv:2601.20189 (2026)
reported_as: The length of the SSE runs generating these results were adapted to achieve a statistical error less than 3 x 10^-8 in the energy (rounded to one digit in the table). [...] The results for L <= 30 represent averages over simulations at beta/L = 32 and 64. [...] The calculations reported here were mostly limited to beta/L <= 64 and system sizes L <= 96, with some limited test results generated also at beta/L = 128 for L = 80, 88, and 96. [...] As an example of the computational effort involved to generate the data presented here, in the case of the L = 96 system at inverse temperature beta = 64L, one full SSE updating sweep with measurements of observables required about 10 s using Intel Xeon Gold 6000-series CPUs. Approximately 1.5 x 10^8 such steps were performed, for a total of about 4 x 10^5 hours of CPU core time, distributed over a large number of CPU cores. In the case of L = 8 at beta = 32L, an updating sweep takes about 1e-3 s and about 2 x 10^11 steps were carried out for a total of about 5 x 10^4 core hours (and this accounted for about half of the statistics for this system size, the remainder coming from beta = 64L runs). [...] The numerical calculations were carried out on the Shared Computing Cluster managed by Boston University's Research Computing Services.

method: mVMC with SU(2) and point group projection
reference: https://journals.aps.org/prb/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevB.104.L220408
reported_as: Supplemental Material, Sec. II.C (many-variable wave function, mVMC): The parameters f_ij are optimised using the stochastic reconfiguration optimization technique [S8] ... In this work, for systems with more than 36 sites, we partially impose translational symmetry directly on the variational parameters f_ij. Namely, we introduce translational symmetry modulo 2 × 2 unit cells sublattice structure and project the 2×2 translations and the point-group symmetries using Eq. (S15). The resulting procedure amounts into 2 × 2 × 6^2 × L^2 variational parameters with L being the number of unit cells in each lattice direction. Such partial translational symmetry imposition is a reasonable compromise between the ability to express complicated wave function and and the required time to learn the wave function. ... Acknowledgments: The mVMC simulations (results section) were supported by the RSF grant (project No. 21-12-00237). The authors acknowledge the usage of computing resources of the federal collective usage center "Complex for simulation and data processing for mega-science facilities" at NRC "Kurchatov Institute", http://ckp.nrcki.ru.

method: Grassmann Variational Monte Carlo (GVMC): CNN backflow + complex RBM neural wave function, Grassmannian Stochastic Reconfiguration (SPRING/Woodbury), ground state |E0> in the (qx,qy,qsf)=(0,0,0)=Gamma sector
reference: Grassmann Variational Monte Carlo with neural wave functions, arXiv:2507.10287
reported_as: Sec. V (Results): For the simulations, we considered the following network hyperparameters: G = 3 stages with B = 2, 2, 8 number of blocks, d = 4, 6, 12 for the 6 x 6 and d = 8, 12, 20 for the 10 x 10, C = 4 for the 6 x 6 and C = 6 for the 10 x 10. The filter sizes are set to K = 3 and K_dw = 5, and the expansion ratio to f = 4. For the RBMs, we employed 16 hidden units for the 6 x 6 and 12 for the 10 x 10. We typically use 2^11 Monte Carlo samples and perform around 5000 SR steps with a learning rate of eta = 0.15/N_s. The QGT inversion is stabilized with a diagonal shift of 10^-3. Finally, parameter updates are performed using the SPRING algorithm [43]. || Sec. VII (Software): All the simulations have been carried out using the software package NetKet [50, 51].
source: Sec. V Results (hyperparameter paragraph), Sec. VII Software
note: samples = 2^11 = 2048 Monte Carlo samples ('typically'), iterations = around 5000 SR steps, both stated once for all simulations in the paper (scope paper). Architecture for the 10x10 lattice: ConvNeXt-style CNN backflow with G = 3 stages of B = 2, 2, 8 blocks, widths d = 8, 12, 20, C = 6 input channels, K = 3, K_dw = 5, f = 4, plus complex RBMs with 12 hidden units; no parameter count given. The run optimises the ground state plus 4 (6x6) or 6 (10x10) excited states jointly in the Grassmann/subspace framework. No hardware, GPU count, wall-clock or GPU-hours stated anywhere (only NetKet and SpinED software).

method: SSE QMC (stochastic series expansion), T -> 0 converged at beta/L = 32 and 64
reference: Sandvik, High-precision ground state parameters of the two-dimensional spin-1/2 Heisenberg model on the square lattice, arXiv:2601.20189 (2026)
reported_as: The length of the SSE runs generating these results were adapted to achieve a statistical error less than 3 x 10^-8 in the energy (rounded to one digit in the table). [...] The results for L <= 30 represent averages over simulations at beta/L = 32 and 64. [...] The calculations reported here were mostly limited to beta/L <= 64 and system sizes L <= 96, with some limited test results generated also at beta/L = 128 for L = 80, 88, and 96. [...] As an example of the computational effort involved to generate the data presented here, in the case of the L = 96 system at inverse temperature beta = 64L, one full SSE updating sweep with measurements of observables required about 10 s using Intel Xeon Gold 6000-series CPUs. Approximately 1.5 x 10^8 such steps were performed, for a total of about 4 x 10^5 hours of CPU core time, distributed over a large number of CPU cores. In the case of L = 8 at beta = 32L, an updating sweep takes about 1e-3 s and about 2 x 10^11 steps were carried out for a total of about 5 x 10^4 core hours (and this accounted for about half of the statistics for this system size, the remainder coming from beta = 64L runs). [...] The numerical calculations were carried out on the Shared Computing Cluster managed by Boston University's Research Computing Services.
source: Sec. II.3 'Tabulated numerical data' (Table 1 note); Sec. II.2 (beta/L limits); Sec. V (computational-effort paragraph before Acknowledgements); Acknowledgements
note: No per-size cost is stated for this row; the paper gives worked examples only for L = 96 (periodic, beta = 64L: ~4e5 CPU core hours, ~1.5e8 sweeps of ~10 s each on Intel Xeon Gold 6000-series CPUs) and L = 8 (periodic, beta = 32L: ~5e4 core hours for about half the statistics), and states that run lengths were adapted to reach an energy error below 3e-8 (periodic Table 1). All calculations ran on Boston University's Shared Computing Cluster (CPU); core counts and wall-clock are not stated ('distributed over a large number of CPU cores').

reported_as: During the training, we use Adam optimizer with batch size 1,024 for all reported results, and we have found that the stochastic reconfiguration (SR) and the plain stochastic gradient descent (SGD) generally produce higher variational energies within the same number of training steps or wall-clock time. Gradient clipping with global norm 1 is applied to alleviate the energy spikes. After the training, each reported variational energy is estimated from 10^6 samples, and its statistical error is too small to be visible in the plots. [...] For bond dimensions chi <= 10, we use learning rate 1e-2 for 10,000 steps, 1e-3 for another 10,000 steps, and finally 1e-4 for 20,000 steps. We manually reduce the learning rate by a factor of 10 if we find the variational energy diverges in the middle of training. For bond dimensions chi > 10, we start from learning rate 1e-3. The training of a tensor-RNN with chi = 64 on the 10 x 10 triangular AFHM takes about 2 days on an Nvidia V100 GPU.

reported_as: Our implementation utilizes Jax [29] to perform automatic differentiation and sampling, alongside the Optax package [30] for optimization. (...) Optimization generally uses around 180 optimization steps with varying and decaying step size (see appendix); gradients are accumulated with 189,000 samples and parameters are updated using a random step with the computed sign [11]. || After optimization, parameters are selected based on the lowest observed average energy. Using this parameter set, observables such as the local energy and electron occupation are measured with approximately 10^6 samples with a thermalization of 10^3 sweeps. || Most of these parameters are in T_l^sigma, with O(N_l * N^2) parameters. || The step sizes during the first 79 steps of optimization is 0.01 and then is lowered to 0.001 for the remaining 100 steps. The optimal point is selected by the lowest energy during the optimization, normally somewhere after the first 80 steps. Optimization was performed with 126 independent walkers contributing to the total sample collection, while the additional measurement of the optimized parameters used 120 walkers. Each measurement was collected after N * N_l Metropolis updates and values reported in the main text were averaged over walkers and a 1000 sweep thermalization time was used. (...) Variance measurement was performed with an additional 10x samples.

reported_as: We typically choose tau = 0.01 in this work, with which we have verified that the Trotter error is below the targeted statistical errors. || In this section, we present results at half-filling. As mentioned, the AFQMC results are numerically exact, as the sign problem is absent because of the particle-hole symmetry. We use a combination of the path-integral approach [40] and the random walk approach [25]. || In this work, we use a special form of the generalized Hartree-Fock (GHF) [34] wave function as TWF in the AFQMC calculations. This will increase the computation time by a factor of 2 to 4 in different portions of algorithm, because now the Slater determinant of up and down spin are coupled. || Earlier calculations were carried out at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory. Most of the calculations were carried out at the Extreme Science and Engineering Discovery Environment (XSEDE), which is supported by National Science Foundation Grant No. ACI-1053575, and the computational facilities at the College of William and Mary.

reference: Neural Network-Augmented Pfaffian Wave-functions for Scalable Simulations of Interacting Fermions, arXiv:2507.10705
reported_as: In most simulations, we utilize a CNN similar to the ResNet in Ref. [42,69] with 16 layers (8 residual blocks), kernel size 3x3, channel number C = 32, and in total around 150K parameters. Among 32 channels, 28 of them are transformed into F~vh with N~ = 14 hidden fermions in the studied spinful system, and the remaining channels are used for the generalized Jastrow factor J(n). The symmetry projection explained in Appendix F is also implemented to improve the accuracy. For simulations in III D, we utilize a GCNN [41] as also described in Appendix F. Unless otherwise specified, the total number of samples in each VMC iteration is fixed at N_s = 16384, and the training takes around 10^4 VMC iterations.

Parameter count is approximate ('around 150K'); iteration count approximate ('around 10^4'); samples = 16384 per VMC iteration. Optimizer: SR solved with MinSR and SPRING (momentum 0.5). No device or wall-clock is stated for these runs; the only hardware statements are Fig. 3 (forward-pass timing of 10^3 parallel HFPS passes on an A6000 GPU, a benchmark, not a training run) and Table IV (training hours on NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs for the L x 4 stripe runs only). reported_as: We typically choose tau = 0.01 in this work, with which we have verified that the Trotter error is below the targeted statistical errors. || In this section, we present results at half-filling. As mentioned, the AFQMC results are numerically exact, as the sign problem is absent because of the particle-hole symmetry. We use a combination of the path-integral approach [40] and the random walk approach [25]. || In this work, we use a special form of the generalized Hartree-Fock (GHF) [34] wave function as TWF in the AFQMC calculations. This will increase the computation time by a factor of 2 to 4 in different portions of algorithm, because now the Slater determinant of up and down spin are coupled. || Earlier calculations were carried out at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory. Most of the calculations were carried out at the Extreme Science and Engineering Discovery Environment (XSEDE), which is supported by National Science Foundation Grant No. ACI-1053575, and the computational facilities at the College of William and Mary.

source: Sec. IV Testing the method; Sec. V; Sec. VI; Fig. 11 caption; Acknowledgments
note: parameters = 65 is the paper's formula for the most general stripe ansatz, 8W + 1 variational parameters, evaluated at the stated stripe width W = 8 (the number 65 itself is not printed; the formula is). Worklist row cites the journal URL (PRB 107, 115133, 2023) = arXiv:2101.07045 (S. Sorella, VAFQMC). No run time, core count, core-hours or per-run sample count is stated for any energy in the paper; the only sample statement (> 3 x 10^5 samples per optimisation iteration) is given for the uniform d-wave ansatz optimisation of Fig. 11 on 16 x 16, not for the stripe runs, so samples is left null. Cost-relevant settings that are stated: twist-averaged boundary conditions with 16 x 16 twists for U/t = 8 and 6 (32 x 32 for U/t = 4, 64 x 64 for U/t = 2, in the uniform-phase study); projection time tau t = 1.3 (U/t = 8), 1.73 (U/t = 6), 2.6 (U/t = 4) at the lowest T_eff; a single Trotter step parameter Delta tau optimised. Hardware only as acknowledgements (Marconi/CINECA via PRACE, HOKUSAI/RIKEN). Individual filling/U energies are tabulated in the Supplementary Information, not in the main arXiv text.

reported_as: According to Eq.(4), for a filling of n=0.875 on 64-site lattices, the parameter numbers for NN and all-site backflow are 286,720 and 3,670,016, respectively. For the 16×16 lattice with NN backflow, the parameter number is 4,587,520. [Sec. III.B; Table III: NN 8×8 286720, NN 4×16 286720, all-site 8×8 3670016, all-site 4×16 3670016, NN 16×16 4587520, with n=0.875 and U=8 under OBC] ... Energy results achieved by wave-functions before and after a Lanczos step are evaluated with the MC sample number in the magnitude of O(4.5×10^4). [Sec. III] ... (1) With a sample size of O(4.5×10^4), the step size is initially set to 2×10^−3 and then reduced to 2×10^−4. (2) With a sample size of O(4.5×10^4), the step size is initially set to 2×10^−3, the sample size is then increased to O(4.5×10^5) while maintaining the step size, and finally, the step size is reduced to 2×10^−4. ... For lattices larger than 64 sites, both strategies require no more than 2×10^4 optimization steps to achieve full convergence. [Sec. III.A] ... X. Liang thanks Eric J. Walter for resource allocations on the William & Mary Sciclone cluster. The author acknowledges William & Mary Research Computing and the Texas Advanced Computing Center (TACC) at The University of Texas at Austin for providing computational resources that have contributed to the results reported within this paper. Part of numerical results were obtained on the Bridges-2 at Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center through allocation (phy240244). [Sec. V Acknowledgement]

method: AFQMC, sign-problem-free at half filling (tau = 0.01, Trotter error below the statistical error)
reference: Qin, Shi & Zhang, Benchmark study of the two-dimensional Hubbard model with auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo method, Phys. Rev. B 94, 085103 (2016), arXiv:1605.09421
device: XSEDE resources (most calculations); Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility (earlier calculations); College of William and Mary facilities (acknowledgement only, no machine or processor named)
reported_as: We typically choose tau = 0.01 in this work, with which we have verified that the Trotter error is below the targeted statistical errors. || In this section, we present results at half-filling. As mentioned, the AFQMC results are numerically exact, as the sign problem is absent because of the particle-hole symmetry. We use a combination of the path-integral approach [40] and the random walk approach [25]. || In this work, we use a special form of the generalized Hartree-Fock (GHF) [34] wave function as TWF in the AFQMC calculations. This will increase the computation time by a factor of 2 to 4 in different portions of algorithm, because now the Slater determinant of up and down spin are coupled. || Earlier calculations were carried out at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory. Most of the calculations were carried out at the Extreme Science and Engineering Discovery Environment (XSEDE), which is supported by National Science Foundation Grant No. ACI-1053575, and the computational facilities at the College of William and Mary.

note: Half-filling AFQMC data of Appendix Table IV (PBC and PBC-APBC, 4x4 to 16x16, U = 2-8). No walker counts, projection times, sample/block counts, core counts, core-hours or wall-clock are stated anywhere for these runs; the only quantitative method setting is the Trotter step tau = 0.01 (with a tau -> 0 extrapolation used only for the TABC data). The GHF trial-wave-function remark is a relative cost (factor 2-4 in computation time), not an absolute one.

reported_as: Our implementation utilizes Jax [29] to perform automatic differentiation and sampling, alongside the Optax package [30] for optimization. (...) Optimization generally uses around 180 optimization steps with varying and decaying step size (see appendix); gradients are accumulated with 189,000 samples and parameters are updated using a random step with the computed sign [11]. || After optimization, parameters are selected based on the lowest observed average energy. Using this parameter set, observables such as the local energy and electron occupation are measured with approximately 10^6 samples with a thermalization of 10^3 sweeps. || Most of these parameters are in T_l^sigma, with O(N_l * N^2) parameters. || The step sizes during the first 79 steps of optimization is 0.01 and then is lowered to 0.001 for the remaining 100 steps. The optimal point is selected by the lowest energy during the optimization, normally somewhere after the first 80 steps. Optimization was performed with 126 independent walkers contributing to the total sample collection, while the additional measurement of the optimized parameters used 120 walkers. Each measurement was collected after N * N_l Metropolis updates and values reported in the main text were averaged over walkers and a 1000 sweep thermalization time was used. (...) Variance measurement was performed with an additional 10x samples.

reported_as: Our implementation utilizes Jax [29] to perform automatic differentiation and sampling, alongside the Optax package [30] for optimization. (...) Optimization generally uses around 180 optimization steps with varying and decaying step size (see appendix); gradients are accumulated with 189,000 samples and parameters are updated using a random step with the computed sign [11]. || After optimization, parameters are selected based on the lowest observed average energy. Using this parameter set, observables such as the local energy and electron occupation are measured with approximately 10^6 samples with a thermalization of 10^3 sweeps. || Most of these parameters are in T_l^sigma, with O(N_l * N^2) parameters. || The step sizes during the first 79 steps of optimization is 0.01 and then is lowered to 0.001 for the remaining 100 steps. The optimal point is selected by the lowest energy during the optimization, normally somewhere after the first 80 steps. Optimization was performed with 126 independent walkers contributing to the total sample collection, while the additional measurement of the optimized parameters used 120 walkers. Each measurement was collected after N * N_l Metropolis updates and values reported in the main text were averaged over walkers and a 1000 sweep thermalization time was used. (...) Variance measurement was performed with an additional 10x samples.

reported_as: Our implementation utilizes Jax [29] to perform automatic differentiation and sampling, alongside the Optax package [30] for optimization. (...) Optimization generally uses around 180 optimization steps with varying and decaying step size (see appendix); gradients are accumulated with 189,000 samples and parameters are updated using a random step with the computed sign [11]. || After optimization, parameters are selected based on the lowest observed average energy. Using this parameter set, observables such as the local energy and electron occupation are measured with approximately 10^6 samples with a thermalization of 10^3 sweeps. || Most of these parameters are in T_l^sigma, with O(N_l * N^2) parameters. || The step sizes during the first 79 steps of optimization is 0.01 and then is lowered to 0.001 for the remaining 100 steps. The optimal point is selected by the lowest energy during the optimization, normally somewhere after the first 80 steps. Optimization was performed with 126 independent walkers contributing to the total sample collection, while the additional measurement of the optimized parameters used 120 walkers. Each measurement was collected after N * N_l Metropolis updates and values reported in the main text were averaged over walkers and a 1000 sweep thermalization time was used. (...) Variance measurement was performed with an additional 10x samples.
source: Sec. II A Implementation Details; Sec. II (parameter scaling); Appendix A Further Computational Details

Parameter count not stated, only the scaling O(N_l * N^2), dominated by the T_l^sigma hopping matrices. method: AFQMC, sign-problem-free at half filling (tau = 0.01, Trotter error below the statistical error)
reference: Qin, Shi & Zhang, Benchmark study of the two-dimensional Hubbard model with auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo method, Phys. Rev. B 94, 085103 (2016), arXiv:1605.09421
device: XSEDE resources (most calculations); Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility (earlier calculations); College of William and Mary facilities (acknowledgement only, no machine or processor named)
reported_as: We typically choose tau = 0.01 in this work, with which we have verified that the Trotter error is below the targeted statistical errors. || In this section, we present results at half-filling. As mentioned, the AFQMC results are numerically exact, as the sign problem is absent because of the particle-hole symmetry. We use a combination of the path-integral approach [40] and the random walk approach [25]. || In this work, we use a special form of the generalized Hartree-Fock (GHF) [34] wave function as TWF in the AFQMC calculations. This will increase the computation time by a factor of 2 to 4 in different portions of algorithm, because now the Slater determinant of up and down spin are coupled. || Earlier calculations were carried out at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory. reference: https://journals.aps.org/prx/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevX.7.031013
reported_as: The many-body wave function of the impurity models is parameterized by the Fork tensor product states (FTPS) [78]. (...) The ground state is found in our calculations by the single-site DMRG algorithm supplied with a subspace expansion [79]. Except for the three-band model with spin-orbital coupling, which has only U(1) symmetry for the charge sector, all calculations are performed under the global U(1) symmetries for the charge and spin sectors. We first perform 30 DMRG sweeps without symmetries with a relatively low bond dimension to find the correct charge and spin sector. Then, the charge and the spin quantum numbers are fixed to be <N_alpha> and <S^z_alpha> for each spin-orbital alpha, respectively. reported_as: For all the system's sizes we use the same number of the training epochs (1500) and the same ViT architecture that comprises 4 layers, 12 attention heads and embedding dimension of 60, which results in ∼1.5×10^5 trainable parameters. method: DMRG, extrapolated in the truncation error (4096-8192 SU(2) states)
reference: Gong, Zhu, Sheng, Motrunich & Fisher, Plaquette ordered phase and quantum phase diagram in the spin-1/2 J1-J2 square Heisenberg model, Phys. Rev. Lett. 113, 027201 (2014), arXiv:1311.5962
reported_as: DMRG energies are obtained by keeping 4096, 6144, and 8192 SU(2) states. reported_as: TABLE I. Benchmark variational energies for the Shastry-Sutherland and J1-J2 models, using deep translationally-symmetry NQS. The corresponding number of parameters, Np, are indicated. J1-J2 (J1 = 1, J2 = 0.5): ConvNext -0.497583(6), Np = 2.6 x 10^5; fViT [16] -0.497634(1), 2.7 x 10^5; ResNet [15] -0.4976921(4), 1.07 x 10^6. || Bringing all of the previous results together, we choose a network of (6,3,3)[2,2] to compute energies for the L = 10 Shastry-Sutherland model and the L = 10 J1-J2 model. || Our optimization protocol makes use of different symmetry stages [16] as shown in fig. 5 (...) We begin the optimization with the bare network, which internally is made to be translationally invariant. We then introduce point group and spin-parity externally (...) First, we symmetrize over the rotational elements of the point group, that is C4 rotations. We then symmetrize over the full point group, adding reflection in the line x = y to the group to be symmetrized over. Finally we add spin parity symmetry (...) Each iteration, we use the SPRING algorithm described in section A to update the parameters. (...) In the numerical experiments for designing the network we typically perform 2500 iterations in each symmetry stage, with a cosine decaying learning rate [82] from 10^-2 to 5 x 10^-3 and a cosine decaying diagonal shift from 10^-2 to 10^-6 in each stage. We use a total of 4092 samples per iteration, with 512 MC chains on each of 8 A100 GPUs (1 sample per chain), each chain performing a single MC sweep of N_MC steps. At the end of the optimization, we freeze the learning rate and diagonal shift, performing 50 additional optimization steps with more samples per chain, discarding half for thermalization. We use 32 chains per GPU and 8196 total samples. To compute an expectation value for the energy we then load in the parameters which gives the minimum energy over these 50 iterations and use 6.4 x 10^5 samples on 32 chains on a single GPU (half of the samples are discarded for thermalization). || This project was provided with computing HPC and storage resources by GENCI at IDRIS thanks to the grants 2023-AD010514908 and 2024-A0170515698 on the supercomputer Jean Zay's V100/A100 partition.

reference: Chen, Hendry, Weinberg & Feiguin, Systematic improvement of neural network quantum states using a Lanczos recursion, arXiv:2206.14307 (2022)
device: Intel E5-2680v4 and AMD Rome 7702 CPU nodes
reported_as: For the neural network, we use psi_KL in all simulations and consider three different values for the number hidden variables M consisting of 2, 2.5 and 3 times of the number of spins N = L^2 in the system. [...] we implement the conjugate gradient method to solve the system of equations, Eq.(12). To stabilize the method, we introduce a ridge parameter lambda = 1e-6. For each training step, we collect 10000 samples to evaluate averages as mentioned in Sec. 3.2 including the variational energy and log derivatives. [...] The typical value for N_skip is from 30 to 100. As for evaluation, we collect 2 x 10^5 samples to calculate the average and statistical error. The learning rate used in the training ranges from 5e-4 to 3e-2. [...] For large L, to save training time, we initialize the parameters W in psi_KL using the parameters trained by means of the cheaper wave function psi_s. All simulations are performed using Eigen and Intel MKL on Intel E5-2680v4 and AMD Rome 7702 CPU nodes.
source: Sec. 3.4 'Implementation details'; Sec. 3.3 ('a good approximation of the ground state can be achieved after hundreds or thousands iterations'); Sec. 5 Limitations ('The computational cost of a single training step scales as O(N_sample x M N^2)')

reported_as: We optimized all models using IT-SWO [25]. method: NQS (CNN+FCN sign-structure ansatz, 2745 parameters, 2000 MC samples), best-performing O-tilde method (Eq.22) with SR
reference: Improving neural network performance for solving quantum sign structure, arXiv:2510.02051
reported_as: For A_theta(sigma), the 2D configuration first passes through a convolutional layer with 64 6 x 6 kernels. We then take absolute value for each element, followed by taking the maximum value for each site across the 64 kernels, and then sum over all sites to get the output. [...] For the phase phi_theta(sigma) we use three fully-connected layers each followed by ReLU [...] The number of neurons in the hidden layers are both 8, and the number of neurons in the output layer is 1. In total, our neural networks have 2745 real-valued parameters. We use 2000 Monte Carlo samples and optimize the network using Nesterov's accelerated gradient method [49] with momentum coefficient mu = 0.5 and learning rate of 0.04. [...] We gratefully acknowledge the use of computational resources at Yale Center for Research Computing. [...] Supplementary Table 2: Hyperparameter setup for the J2/J1 = 0.5 case: O~ Method (SR): learning rate 0.04 (adaptive), m value 4, beta value 0.2.
source: Sec. II 'Neural network' (architecture paragraph); Acknowledgments; Supplementary Material Sec. 1.6 Tables 1-2

reference: F. Mezzacapo, N. Schuch, M. Boninsegni, and J. I. Cirac, Ground-state properties of quantum many-body systems: entangled-plaquette states and variational monte carlo, New Journal of Physics 11, 083026 (2009). (cited as ref [60] in arXiv:2510.02051)
reported_as: In a typical calculation, we start with 2 x 2 plaquettes; once the energy has converged, the size of the plaquettes is increased to improve the estimate. The number of coefficients which need be stored in memory for a spin-1/2 system is N x 2^(l1 x l2), and can be reduced taking into account problem-dependent symmetries. For each optimization step, a few thousands updates are necessary to get a rough estimate of the energy and efficiently move the coefficients along the gradient. [...] The relative error is already small (less than 1%) for 2 x 2 plaquettes and reaches a value < 1e-3 when 4 x 4 plaquettes are used. [...] TABLE IV: GS energy per site (in units of J1) for the J1 - J2 model on a square lattice (with PBC) comprising 36 sites. [...] J2/J1 = 0.5: This work -0.4985(2), Exact -0.5038.

method: ViT with Spatial Attention, zero-variance extrapolation
reference: Approaching the Thermodynamic Limit with Neural-Network Quantum States, arXiv:2602.02665
device: NVIDIA GH200
reported_as: The Vision Transformer architecture used in this work comprises h = 12 attention heads, n_l = 8 layers, and an embedding dimension of d = 72, resulting in approximately P ~ 4.5 x 10^5 trainable parameters for different system sizes, from L = 18 to L = 42. The input spin configuration sigma is divided into n non-overlapping patches of size b x b [13], each embedded into R^d through a learnable linear transformation (...) In particular, we set b = 3 for the triangular lattice, which is compatible with the Neel 120 degree antiferromagnetic order and b = 4 for the square lattice (see Section IV). || Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) optimizations employing M = 2^14 samples for the stochastic estimates were carried out using SR [58] with the linear algebra trick being in the regime P >> M [11, 20] enhanced with SPRING [107]. The optimization proceeded in three stages: 5000 steps without symmetry summation, followed by 500 steps including translational symmetries, and a final 100 steps with both rotational and reflection symmetries restored. The initial learning rate was set to eta = 5 x 10^-3 and gradually decreased during training. || The numerical experiments performed in this work required 25000 hours on GH200 GPUs. However, we point out that the preceding results obtained with other variational approaches, such as Gutzwiller Projected and RNN wave functions (see Table I), can be achieved with fewer than 1000 GPU hours. || This work was supported as part of the "Swiss AI initiative" by a grant from the Swiss National Supercomputing Centre (CSCS) under project ID a117 on Alps. RR and LLV acknowledge the CINECA award under the ISCRA initiative for the availability of high-performance computing resources and support.
source: Sec. V B Architecture and Optimization Details; Acknowledgments (25000 GH200 GPU-hours)
note: gpu_hours = 25000 is the total for ALL numerical experiments in the paper (triangular lattice L = 18-42 plus this 20x20 J1-J2 run), not for this row. parameters = "approximately 4.5 x 10^5", stated for the triangular sizes L = 18-42; the 20x20 square run uses the same architecture (h = 12, n_l = 8, d = 72) with patch size b = 4, but its own count is not restated. iterations = 5000 + 500 + 100 stated stages (sum); samples = 2^14 per step. Optimization protocol is the paper-wide description. This row is the zero-variance extrapolation of the three symmetry stages (Fig. 5), not a separate run.

reported_as: DMRG energies are obtained by keeping 4096, 6144, and 8192 SU(2) states. [endnote 65]

note: Extrapolated (M -> infinity) from the 4096/6144/8192 SU(2)-state runs (about 16000/24000/32000 U(1) states) by a straight-line fit in truncation error; no single bond dimension applies. No wall-clock, core count or memory stated anywhere in the paper or supplement. Torus L=8.

reported_as: Appendix A9 Optimization parameters: We optimized all models using IT-SWO[25]. We used 30 iterations in the inner loop and chose imaginary time constant β based on the relative scale of the energy spectrum for different problems (Table V: Triangular N=108, β = 0.01). Each iteration was performed using adam optimizer[24] with b1 = 0.9; b2 = 0.99 and learning rate that was decayed exponentially with the rate of 0.1 over 8∗10^5 updates starting with 7∗10^−4 ... We optimized all GNN models for 8∗10^5 iterations (≈ 26000 IT-SWO steps). For larger system sizes we initialized the weights with values from smaller system sizes. ... All models were optimized using Google's Cloud TPU v4. All models trained within a day. ... Appendix A8b: All results were computed using MCMC using 2∗10^5 samples from equilibrated Markov chains. ... Appendix A8c: To measure computational efficiency we have timed the process of evaluating 7200 batches of 32 basis configuration within a MCMC process. The GNN-2 model took 17.4 seconds to accomplish this task, while our unstructured ResNet baseline finishes in 2.14 seconds. ... Appendix A6a: Node and edge functions of the Encoder, Processor and Decoder are implemented as MLPs with 3 hidden layers with ReLU activations. The node and edge embeddings have size 64, while hidden layers width 128. We use 6 message passing steps with residual connections in the Processor.

reported_as: TABLE I caption: [...] The cumulative training time, hereafter, is reported in hh:mm:ss format. We also report our runtimes for training the 1D LRU using a single H100 95GB GPU. For reference, this model consists of 3 layers with d = d_h = 64 and has around 75,000 variational parameters. || TABLE I row N = 10: Time per training step (ms) 10; Number of training steps 30000; Cumulative training time 00:18:23. || Sec. reported_as: Fig. 3 shows the DMRG approximation E(|psi*_MPS>) for the (unknown) ground state energy of the transverse field Ising Hamiltonian (20) on a 20 by 20 square lattice, at a near-critical magnetic field strength of B = 3.0 and exactly encoded in an MPO with bond dimension D' = 22. [...] At bond dimension D = 2^15 = 32,768 our simulations already reached the maximum level of achievable accuracy within single precision arithmetic. [...] Figure 3. Convergence of the DMRG ground state energy per site as a function of bond dimension D for the critical transverse field Ising model on a 20x20 lattice, leading to an energy density of -3.18197(2). reference: https://journals.aps.org/prresearch/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevResearch.5.L032001
reported_as: During the training, we use Adam optimizer with batch size 1,024 for all reported results, and we have found that the stochastic reconfiguration (SR) and the plain stochastic gradient descent (SGD) generally produce higher variational energies within the same number of training steps or wall-clock time. Gradient clipping with global norm 1 is applied to alleviate the energy spikes. After the training, each reported variational energy is estimated from 10^6 samples, and its statistical error is too small to be visible in the plots. [...] For bond dimensions chi <= 10, we use learning rate 1e-2 for 10,000 steps, 1e-3 for another 10,000 steps, and finally 1e-4 for 20,000 steps. We manually reduce the learning rate by a factor of 10 if we find the variational energy diverges in the middle of training. For bond dimensions chi > 10, we start from learning rate 1e-3. The training of a tensor-RNN with chi = 64 on the 10 x 10 triangular AFHM takes about 2 days on an Nvidia V100 GPU.

reference: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09077
reported_as: The total set of variational parameters theta = (M_mu i, theta_BF, theta_J) are all optimized simultaneously using Variational Monte Carlo and Stochastic Reconfiguration [84]. To accelerate the optimization convergence of our Neural Slater-Backflow-Jastrow ansatz, we initialize the orbital parameters with converged parameters of a Hartree-Fock optimization. For smaller systems (i.e. L = 4) we use shallow backflow CNN networks with one hidden layer and 32 features. For larger and more challenging systems such as L = 8, 10 we construct a residual CNN with 5 convolutional layers and 16 features per filter. [...] To access low-lying energy states, we use the latter residual CNN architecture regardless of the system size. Our deep CNNs use complex-valued weights for the feature maps. [...] We optimize multiple CNN backflow transformation models in parallel, corresponding to the N_f orbitals, ensuring efficient and scalable processing. For the optimization, we use a learning rate of 0.0075. The optimization is carried out using the SR preconditioner with a diagonal shift of 0.001, and we use 4096 Monte Carlo samples.
source: Supplementary Note I (Numerical details and backflow architecture)
note: One blanket statement for the whole paper: 4096 MC samples. This row is the non-backflow Slater-Jastrow ansatz, so the CNN backflow spec does not apply; its parameters are the Jastrow W_{d(ij)} plus the N_f x N_s orbital matrix (no count given). No hardware, wall-clock or iteration count in the paper.
